title: Google Meet Screen Share Not Working: How to Fix It
body_md:
![Google Meet Help page on presenting during a video meeting](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/google-meet-screen-share-not-working-how-to-fix-it/1.png)
*Google's official Present during a video meeting help page ([source](https://support.google.com/meet/answer/9308856))*

On a Mac, a missing screen-recording permission can prevent sharing. If you missed the permission prompt, check **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording** for the browser, then quit and reopen it before rejoining. If the Present option is missing or disabled, the host or a Workspace admin may have restricted sharing — Google's own help page says screen sharing may be disabled for you due to admin settings or meeting host controls. See [Google's presentation guidance](https://support.google.com/meet/answer/9308856).

## Why This Happens

Screen sharing breaks in Meet for a handful of predictable reasons:

- **Missing OS-level screen recording permission.** macOS blocks apps from capturing your display until you explicitly allow it, and the permission only takes effect after the browser restarts.
- **Permissions that "look" enabled but aren't.** After a macOS or Chrome update, an already-on toggle can stop working and needs to be removed and re-added.
- **The host turned sharing off.** Meeting hosts can stop participants from sharing their screen. When that happens, the Present option isn't available to you.
- **Wrong entry point.** If you click Present in the green room before joining, you join in a present-only mode. On mobile, Google describes it plainly: when you join to present, only your window or application is shown in the meeting, and no audio or other video is shared.
- **No audio in the share.** This isn't broken sharing, it's the wrong share type. A presented Chrome tab shares that tab's audio by default, while a window or entire screen needs **Also share system audio** enabled.
- **Browser or extension conflicts.** Old browser builds, aggressive privacy extensions, or Meet-specific extensions can block the capture prompt.

## Step-by-Step Fixes

### 1. Grant (or reset) screen recording permission on macOS

Google's own guidance for permission prompts: if you missed the initial dialog to allow permissions, you'll need to update your system settings.

1. Open **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording** (older macOS: System Preferences → Security & Privacy → Privacy → Screen Recording).
2. Toggle on your browser or the Google Meet app. If it's not listed, use the **+** button to add it.
3. Authenticate with your password or Touch ID if prompted.
4. Choose **Quit & Reopen** when macOS asks. The permission won't apply until the browser fully restarts.
5. Rejoin the meeting and try **Present now** again.

**If the toggle was already on and sharing still fails:** select the browser, hit the **–** button to remove it, then add it back and restart. macOS updates can leave this permission in a stale state.

### 2. Check host controls

If the Present button is missing or grayed out for you but works for others, the host has locked sharing. A host or co-host can fix it in seconds: join the meeting, click **Host controls** at the bottom right, and in the side panel toggle **Share their screen** on. On mobile, tap the screen, tap More, tap **Host controls**, and turn **Share their screen** on or off at the bottom. Note that Host Management has to be turned on for this control to exist.

If you're not the host, message them in chat — you can't override this yourself.

### 3. Make sure you actually joined the meeting

Don't click Present from the pre-join screen unless you mean to. That path joins you present-only, with no audio or other video shared. Join the meeting normally first, then share.

### 4. Use the right share type

At the bottom, click **Present now**, then pick **A tab**, **A window**, or **Your entire screen**. A few gotchas:

- **Video or audio playback?** Share a **tab** — tab audio goes out by default. For a desktop app, pick a window or your screen and enable the system audio toggle in the selection dialog. Window and screen audio has OS requirements: Windows 11 or later, or macOS 14.2 or later.
- **Multiple monitors?** "Your entire screen" asks you to pick *one* display. Pick the one your content is actually on.
- **Wrong tab showing?** Select the tab you want and click **Share this tab instead** on the banner.
- **Someone else presenting?** You don't have to wait. You can present even if someone else is already presenting — Meet allows up to 10 simultaneous presentations in a meeting.

### 5. Swap or reset the browser

Meet's deepest integration is with Chrome, and the newer system-audio sharing path depends on a current Chrome build. Try, in order:

1. Fully quit and reopen the browser (not just close the tab).
2. Update to the latest version.
3. Disable extensions — ad blockers, privacy tools, and Meet add-ons are common offenders. Some Chrome extensions for Meet can interfere with expected functionality, and disabling them is the recommended fix.
4. Test in an incognito/private window with extensions off.
5. Try a different profile or a different browser to isolate the problem.

### 6. Rule out the network and the stop button

If you're clearly presenting on your end but attendees see a frozen or black screen, bandwidth is one possible cause, not a diagnosis. Turn off your camera, close bandwidth-heavy apps, switch from Wi-Fi to Ethernet if you can, or stop and restart the share. To stop cleanly, click **Stop Presenting** in the Meet window, or click **You are presenting → Stop presenting** at the bottom right. On mobile, tap Stop sharing, then OK.

### 7. Ask your admin

If nothing works and you're on a work or school account, sharing may be disabled at the organization level. Google's admin documentation is blunt about it: if the "Allow users to share their screen" setting is turned off, users can't share their screen, even in meetings hosted by other organizations. Your IT admin can confirm and change it.

## How to Prevent It Next Time

- **Grant the macOS permission before you need it.** Check it before important meetings and recheck after major OS updates.
- **Re-check permissions after big OS updates.** These toggles can reset or go stale.
- **Do a 30-second dry run** before any important demo — join a solo meeting from your own link and test Present now.
- **Keep a clean browser profile for meetings** with extensions kept to a minimum.
- **If you host recurring calls,** check your host controls once and confirm **Share their screen** is on. If you turn presentations off in recurring meetings or meetings that use the same code, the setting is saved for the next scheduled meeting.

*Updated October 2026: this guide is written from Google's official documentation and public reports, not a controlled diagnostic test.*

## My Take

My read is that most "Meet screen share not working" cases aren't Meet's fault at all — they're macOS permission state or a host toggle. Those two account for the failures that look most alarming (no Present button, a dialog that never appears), and both are fixed in under a minute once you know where to look. Everything else is slower to diagnose and rarer.

I think the single most useful habit here is the dry run. The permission flow requires a browser restart, which is exactly the thing you can't do thirty seconds before a client demo. Checking it the day before costs nothing.

The audio story has genuinely improved, and I'd stop treating tab-sharing as the only option. Google now supports system audio from a window or your whole screen, but it's gated on Windows 11 or macOS 14.2 or later and a current Chrome — so if you're on an older machine, sharing a tab is still the move.

Fair point against me: not every frozen-screen complaint is user error. Bandwidth, VPNs, and corporate proxies really do break capture, and Meet gives you almost no diagnostic signal when they do. That's a design gap, and telling people to "check their connection" is weak advice when the app could just say what failed.

One caveat I'd flag: if your admin has locked presenting at the org level, don't go hunting for workarounds. That's a policy decision, usually a security one, and I'm not an IT or compliance professional — ask your admin rather than trying to route around them.
